summary: Defines MIB objects for administering SNMP parties, the entities in the party-based SNMP security model, including how they are represented and managed. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A list of settings that tell a network device which helpers it trusts and what they may do.

questions: how does snmp party authentication work
why was the party model replaced
subtitle: Management objects for administering SNMP party-based security

tldr.problem: SNMP networks needed a way to define and manage parties, the security entities in the party-based SNMP security model that determine who can access what.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines MIB tables for SNMP party administration: one for public party information (clocks and identifiers), one for secret authentication and privacy parameters, one for access control rules, and one for managing which objects each party can access.
tldr.outcome: The party-based SNMP security model was later replaced by SNMPv3, which uses a different user-based security model (USM). This RFC is Historic.

today: RFC 1353 is Historic. The party-based SNMP security model it defines was an early approach to securing SNMP, but was later superseded by SNMPv3, which introduced the user-based security model (USM). SNMPv3 became the standard security framework for SNMP and is documented in RFC 3414 and related RFCs. The party-based model is no longer used in modern SNMP implementations.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 1353 defines Management Information Base (MIB) objects for administering SNMP parties, which are security entities in the party-based SNMP security model. Parties represent the protocol principals (senders and receivers) participating in SNMP communications.

This MIB allows network administrators to define and manage parties in a standardized way using SNMP itself. The document is part of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which includes the SMI (Structure of Management Information), the MIB (management objects), and SNMP (the protocol used to access them).
sections.eli5: SNMP is a way network devices talk to management tools. This RFC says how to define and keep track of which helpers (parties) the device trusts and what they can do.

sections.title: SNMP Party Structure and Security Framework
sections.content:
A party is identified by an Object Identifier and represents an SNMP principal that can send and receive management protocol messages. Parties are characterized by their authentication clock (for message sequencing), transport address, and associated authentication and privacy protocols.

The party-based security model uses authentication to verify that a message comes from a claimed party and has not been modified in transit. It uses privacy (encryption) to prevent unauthorized eavesdropping on management traffic. Different parties can use different combinations of authentication and privacy protocols, ranging from no authentication and no privacy to full authentication with DES privacy.
sections.eli5: A party is like a trusted coworker. For each one, you record their address, how to verify they really are who they claim, and how to keep your messages private when talking to them.

sections.title: Database Tables and Organization
sections.content:
The RFC defines four tables for party administration, organized in separate branches of the MIB tree for security reasons:

Party Public Database: Contains public information about parties including their identifiers and authentication clocks. This is readable by unauthenticated queries because the clock value is needed for re-establishing clock synchronization.

Party Secrets Database: Contains secret authentication and privacy parameters. Positioned in a separate tree branch where access control can restrict reading to only authenticated and privacy-protected queries.

SNMP Access Control Database: Defines which parties have access to which objects and what operations (read, write) each party is permitted.

MIB View Database: Defines which portions of the MIB are visible to each party, allowing fine-grained access control.
sections.eli5: The system keeps four separate lists: who the parties are, their secret passwords, what each party is allowed to do, and what information each party can see.

sections.title: Object Instance Identification
sections.content:
All four tables use Object Identifier values for identification. For the Party Public and Secrets databases, the party identifier itself is the index variable. For the Access Control and Views databases, two index variables are defined, both with Object Identifier syntax.

Instance identifiers are formed according to RFC 1212 conventions: for an object identifier-valued index, the instance identifier includes the number of sub-identifiers in the value (the first sub-identifier) followed by each individual sub-identifier. This allows objects to be uniquely named and distinguished at different levels in the management hierarchy.
sections.eli5: Each entry in the tables has a unique name based on the party's identifier or a combination of party and object identifiers, similar to how files have unique paths in a directory.

sections.title: Authentication and Privacy Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC defines identifiers for several authentication and privacy protocols that parties can use:

  • noAuth: Parties using no authentication (anyone can claim to be them)
  • md5AuthProtocol: MD5-based message authentication with a 1-second granularity authentication clock
  • noPriv: No privacy (messages are sent unencrypted)
  • desPrivProtocol: DES privacy for encryption of management traffic

Parties are also associated with transport domains, such as rfc1351Domain for SNMP over UDP. Proxy domains indicate whether a party operates locally or proxies to other systems.
sections.eli5: Different parties can use different security levels: some don't verify who they are, some use special codes to prove identity, some send messages in secret code, and some do both.

sections.title: Legacy Status and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 1353 defines the MIB for the party-based SNMP security model, which was one of the early attempts to add strong security to SNMP. The party-based model allowed fine-grained definition of authentication and privacy policies.

However, this security framework was later replaced by SNMPv3, which introduced a user-based security model (USM) instead of the party-based model. SNMPv3 also added the SNMP engine concept and more sophisticated key management. This RFC is Historic because the party-based security model it documents is no longer in use in modern SNMP implementations.
sections.eli5: This was an early try at adding security to SNMP. Later, a better method called SNMPv3 was invented, so this older method is no longer used.
